title: Household Orchestra
goal: Your kid builds a piece of music out of exactly five objects from around the house. No instruments, no lessons. They find every sound hiding in those five things, build a rhythm, shape it into a real piece and perform it for the family. The five-object limit is what makes it creative.
need: Five objects that make a sound: pots, wooden spoons, a tin, a box, a jar of dried beans, rubber bands, a comb
A bowl or box to stretch rubber bands over
Glasses with water and a spoon, if your kid is gentle (optional)
A phone to record the performance (optional)

lesson.text: Music is sound with a pattern. Random noise becomes a rhythm once something repeats.
lesson.before: Bang, crash, tap, rattle, bang bang.

model.line: Tap the box on every count: 1, 2, 3, 4.
Shake the beans on count 3 only: tap, tap, shake, tap.
Play it 4 times in a row without stopping.
A steady beat, a pattern on top, repeated. That's a rhythm.

lesson.modelNote: The first try had no beat, so nothing could repeat. Once the box keeps the count, the beans have somewhere to land. Every song your kid knows is built on that same idea.

academics.subject: Music
academics.text: rhythm, layers, a piece with a shape

howTo.intro: Expect noise, and maybe a cheese grater played with a fork. Your job is to hold the line at five objects and keep your own ideas out of it. Kids build a piece by playing it over and over, so let the repeats happen, even the loud ones.

plan.what: Gather the five and find every sound (Steps 1 and 2).
Build a rhythm and compose the piece (Steps 3 and 4).
Perform it for whoever is home (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They want a sixth object, then a seventh
troubleshoot.a: Hold the line. With the whole house, nothing feels special. With five, every choice counts.

troubleshoot.q: The rhythm falls apart when they add a layer
troubleshoot.a: That happens to real musicians too. Go back to the steady beat alone, then add the next sound again.

skills.name: Listening
skills.text: hearing high, low, short and long

steps.title: Gather your five instruments
steps.why: The limit is what makes every choice count.
steps.kid: Your kid hunts the house for exactly five objects that make a sound and are okay to play. The Instrument ideas card in the Orchestra Toolkit at the end of the guide helps: try to get a mix, like something to hit, something to shake and something to scrape.
steps.you: Hold them to five, and let the choices be theirs. Check that everything is safe to bang on.
ask: Why did you pick these five?
Which one will make the most interesting sound?
steps.tip: A mix of kinds makes a better band: one drum, one shaker, one scraper, one with strings, one wild card.

levels.explore: Pick five things that make noise.
levels.develop: Pick five with at least 3 different kinds of sound.
levels.extend: Build one instrument, like rubber bands stretched over a box, as one of the five.

steps.title: Find every sound
steps.why: Each object hides more than one sound.
steps.kid: Your kid explores each object: tap it, shake it, scrape it, hit it soft, hit it hard, on the rim, in the middle. They sort the sounds into high and low, short and long. Then they test the High or low card: does a bigger or tighter thing sound higher or lower?
steps.you: Stay curious and out of the way. The best sound is usually one they find by accident.
ask: How many different sounds can you get from one object?
steps.tip: Try water glasses: tap each gently with a spoon. More water makes a lower note. Line them up from high to low.

levels.develop: Find 3 or more sounds from each, and sort them high to low.
levels.extend: Tune 3 objects to a high, a middle and a low note. Then touch each one while it rings: what do you feel, and what happens to the sound when you grab it?

steps.title: Build a rhythm
steps.why: A steady beat holds everything together.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one object for a steady beat and counts 1, 2, 3, 4 over and over. Then they add a second sound on some of the counts in a pattern that repeats. Once that's solid, they can layer a third.
steps.you: Clap along if they invite you. Don't take over the beat.
ask: What's your steady beat, and what sits on top of it?
Can you keep the pattern going for a whole minute?
steps.tip: A rest counts too. Tap, tap, (nothing), tap. Silence is part of the rhythm.

levels.explore: Tap a steady beat while you count out loud to 4, and add one shake on count 1.
levels.develop: Layer 2 sounds over the beat and keep it going for a minute.
levels.extend: Play a pattern that repeats every 3 counts over a beat of 4. After how many counts do they start together again, and why that number?

steps.title: Compose the piece
steps.why: A piece has a shape. It goes somewhere.
steps.kid: Your kid shapes their rhythms into a piece with a beginning, a middle and an end, using a shape from the Piece shapes card, like quiet, then loud and busy, then quiet again. They give it a name and a feeling: a thunderstorm, a busy kitchen, a robot waking up.
steps.you: Treat it like a real composition, because it is. Ask where it starts and where it ends.
ask: How does your piece start, and how does it end?
If your piece were a place or a feeling, what would it be?
steps.tip: No need to write it down. The plan can live in their head and hands. It just has to go somewhere.

levels.explore: Play a start, a middle and an end.
levels.develop: Give it a name, a feeling and a quiet-loud-quiet shape.
levels.extend: Write a simple score with symbols for each sound, so someone else could play it.

steps.title: Perform it
steps.why: Music is meant to be heard.
steps.kid: Your kid sets up their five instruments, announces the name of the piece and performs it start to finish for whoever is home. If they make a mistake, they keep playing. Then they take a bow.
steps.you: Sit down, give it your full attention and clap like you mean it. Record it if they'd like to keep it.
ask: How did it feel to perform it?
What part are you most proud of?
steps.tip: Playing through a mistake is a real skill. Most audiences never notice if you don't stop.

levels.explore: Play the piece for one person.
levels.develop: Record it, listen back together, change one part, then play it again for the family.
levels.extend: Teach one part to a sibling or parent, and perform it as a duet.

reference.title: Orchestra Toolkit
reference.intro: Instrument ideas from the kitchen, why some things sound high and others low, how to build a rhythm and shapes for a piece.

dried beans or rice in a jar
a grater and a fork, a comb

a pot lid, spoons on a string

items.ask: Do you have at least 3 kinds?

items.name: High or low?
items.ask: Can you play a high, a middle and a low sound?

items.name: Piece shapes

after.label: Musician's rules
lines: Start on purpose, end on purpose.

conclusion.headline: This morning, those were just pots and spoons.
conclusion.text: Ask them which glass sang lowest and why. They'll tell you it was the fullest one, and they found that out by ear. Then ask them to play the piece again. They probably can, from memory, because they built it beat by beat.
conclusion.celebrate: Say the name of their piece back to them and tell them the exact moment you liked: 'When the beans came in on three, it sounded like rain starting.'
extensions: Swap in five new objects and compose a second piece
Start a family band where everyone brings one instrument
Record the piece and add a second layer on top
Play along with a favourite song using only the five instruments

signs: They tap rhythms on tables and count beats
They notice high and low sounds around the house
They make things from what's around instead of asking for new stuff
makeItReal: In a waiting room, hand them three things from your bag and give them one minute to make a beat. Then it's your turn to copy it.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
